source_text: Alypius episcopus ecclesiae catholicae epistulam recitauit: Honorabili ac dilectissimo filio, uiro clarissimo et spectabili, tribuno et notario Marcellino Aurelius, Siluanus et uniuersi episcopi catholici. Edicto spectabilitatis tuae, quo nostrae collationis tranquillitati quietique seruandae et ueritati manifestandae ac muniendae consultum est, in omnibus nos consentire, sicut admonere dignatus es, per has litteras intimamus. illo etiam ueritate confisi nos uinculo condicionis obstringimus, ut, si nobis hi cum quibus agimus demonstrare potuerint, cum secundum dei promissa populi christiani usque quaque crescendo iam magnam partem orbis implessent et in ceteram dilatarentur implendam, subito ecclesiam Christi nescio quorum quos isti accusant peccatorum perisse contagione et in sola parte Donati remansisse, si hoc, ut dictum est, demonstrare potuerint, nullos apud eos honores episcopatus requiremus, sed eorum sequemur pro sola salute consilium, quibus tanti gratiam beneficii pro cognita ueritate debebimus. si autem nos potius ualuerimus ostendere ecclesiam Christi omnium non solum Africanarum, sed etiam transmarinarum prouinciarum, multarum gentium spatia feracissima populorum copia iam tenentem et sicut scriptum est toto mundo fructificantem atque crescentem, nullorum hominum sibi commixtorum peccatis perire potuisse, si denique ipsorum, quos tunc accusare uoluerunt potius quam conuincere ualuerunt, quaestionem definitam, quamuis non in eis ecclesia consistat, et Caecilianum innocentem, illos autem uiolentos et calumniosos esse iudicatos ab eo imperatore, ad cuius examen cuius examen crirainationes suas ultro accusando miserunt, postremo si, quidquid de peccatis quorumlibet hominum dixerint, uel humanis documentis uel diuinis probauerimus aut eorum innocentiam falsis criminibus appetitam aut Christi ecclesiam, cuius communioni cohaeremus, nullis eorum delictis esse destructam, sic eius nobiscum teneant unitatem, ut non solum uiam salutis inueniant, sed nec honorem episcopatus amittant. neque enim in eis diuinae sacramenta ueritatis, sed commenta humani detestamur erroris, quibus sublatis fraternum pectus complectemur christiana nobis caritate coniunctum, quod nunc dolemus dissensione diabolica separatum. poterit quippe unusquisque nostrum honoris sibi socio copulato uicissim sedere eminentius, sicut peregrino episcopo iuxta considente collega. hoc cum alternis basilicis utrimque conceditur utroque alterum cum honore mutuo praeueniente, quia, ubi praeceptio caritatis dilatauerit corda, possessio pacis non fit angusta, ut uno eorum defuncto deinceps iam singulis singuli pristino more succedant. nec nouum aliquid fiet; nam hoc ex ipsius separationis exordio in eis, qui damnato nefariae dissensionis errore unitatis dulcedinem uel sero sapuerunt, catholica dilectio custodiuit. aut si forte populi christiani singulis delectantur episcopis et duorum consortium inusitata rerum facie tolerare non possunt, utrique de medio discedamus et ecclesiis singulis damnata schismatis causa in unitate pacifica constitutis ab episcopis singulis in ecclesiis singulis annuentibus unitati factae per loca necessaria singuli constituantur episcopi.
thought_title: The Catholic bishops' letter to Marcellinus
orientation: Alypius, Catholic bishop of Thagaste, reads aloud the letter that the Catholic bishops sent to Marcellinus, the imperial tribune and notary who judged the Conference of Carthage.
pass_a_gloss: Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, read the letter: To the honorable and most beloved son, the most distinguished and eminent man, tribune and notary Marcellinus, Aurelius, Silvanus and all the Catholic bishops. By the edict of your eminence, by which provision was made for preserving the tranquility and quiet of our conference and for making clear and defending the truth, we make known through this letter that we agree in all things, as you deigned to advise. Trusting also in that truth, we bind ourselves by the bond of a condition, that if those with whom we are dealing can demonstrate to us that, when according to the promises of God the Christian peoples had already filled a great part of the world by growing everywhere and were spreading out to fill the rest, suddenly the Church of Christ perished by the contagion of the sins of I know not whom, whom these men accuse, and remained only in the party of Donatus, if they can demonstrate this, as has been said, we will seek no honors of bishopric among them, but we will follow their counsel for salvation alone, to whom we will owe the grace of so great a benefit for the truth that has been recognized. But if we rather are able to show that the Church of Christ, already holding the most fertile expanses of many peoples with a multitude of peoples, not only of the African provinces but also of the overseas provinces, and as it is written, bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, could not have perished by the sins of any men mixed with it, if finally the question of those very men whom they then wanted to accuse rather than were able to convict has been settled, although the Church does not consist in them, and that Caecilian was judged innocent, but those men violent and slanderous, by that emperor to whose examination they sent their accusations by accusing of their own accord, finally if, whatever they may say about the sins of any men, we prove either by human documents or by divine ones either that their innocence was attacked by false charges or that the Church of Christ, to whose communion we cling, has not been destroyed by any of their offenses, let them so hold unity with us that they not only find the way of salvation, but also do not lose the honor of bishopric. For we do not detest in them the sacraments of divine truth, but the fabrications of human error, and when these are removed, we will embrace the brotherly breast joined to us by Christian love, which we now grieve is separated by diabolical dissension. For each one of us will be able, with a colleague joined to him in honor, to sit in turn more prominently, as when a foreign bishop sits beside him as a colleague. This is granted on both sides when the basilicas are alternated, each one outdoing the other with mutual honor, because where the command of love has widened hearts, the possession of peace does not become narrow, so that when one of them has died, thereafter single bishops succeed single bishops according to the old custom. Nor will anything new happen; for this from the very beginning of the separation the Catholic love preserved in those who, having condemned the error of wicked dissension, tasted the sweetness of unity even if late. Or if perhaps the Christian peoples delight in single bishops and cannot tolerate the partnership of two because of the unusual appearance of the matter, let both of us withdraw from the middle, and with the cause of schism condemned, with the churches established in peaceful unity, with single bishops in single churches consenting to unity, let single bishops be appointed in each place as necessary.

choices.why: Standard rendering of late Roman honorific titles for a high imperial official; 'spectabilis' is a specific rank title.
Marcellinus's official titles; 'notarius' is an imperial secretary, not a modern notary.
Preserves the legal metaphor of a binding stipulation; 'condition' keeps the conditional nature of the offer.

choices.english: only in the party of Donatus
choices.why: Uses the glossary term 'Donatist party' structure while keeping the literal 'parte' as 'party'.
'Commenta' means invented things or fabrications; 'fabrications' captures the sense of human invention opposed to divine truth.
Literal rendering of the metaphor of embracing the breast/heart of a brother; keeps the physical image of embrace.

bible_refs.note: sicut scriptum est toto mundo fructificantem atque crescentem

pass_b_english: Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, read aloud a letter: "To our honorable and most beloved son, the most distinguished and eminent man, tribune and notary Marcellinus: Aurelius, Silvanus, and all the Catholic bishops. By these letters we make known that we agree in everything with your eminence's edict, by which provision was made for preserving the tranquility and quiet of our conference and for making the truth clear and secure, as you were kind enough to advise. Trusting in that truth, we also bind ourselves by the bond of a condition: if those with whom we are dealing can demonstrate to us that, when the Christian people had already grown everywhere according to God's promises and filled a great part of the world and were spreading out to fill the rest, the Church of Christ suddenly perished by the contagion of the sins of certain men whom they accuse, and remained only in the Donatist party—if, as I said, they can demonstrate this, we will seek no honors of a bishopric among them, but we will follow their counsel for salvation alone, since we will owe them the grace of so great a benefit for the truth we have recognized. But if we are able to show instead that the Church of Christ, already holding the most fertile expanses of many nations with a multitude of peoples, not only in the African provinces but also in those across the sea, and, as it is written, bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, as it is written, could not have perished through the sins of any men mixed in with it; if, finally, the question of those very men whom they wanted to accuse rather than were able to convict has been settled—although the Church does not consist in them—and Caecilian was judged innocent, while those men were judged violent and slanderous by that emperor to whose examination they sent their accusations by their own choice; and if, after all this, whatever they say about the sins of any men, we prove either by human documents or by divine ones that their innocence was attacked with false charges, or that the Church of Christ, to whose communion we cling, has not been destroyed by any of their offenses—then let them hold unity with us in such a way that they not only find the way of salvation but do not lose the honor of a bishopric. For we do not detest in them the sacraments of divine truth, but the fabrications of human error. When those are removed, we will embrace a brotherly breast joined to us by Christian love, which we now grieve is separated by diabolical dissension. Each one of us, joined with a colleague in honor, will be able to sit in turn in the more prominent seat, as when a foreign bishop sits beside a colleague. This is granted to both sides in alternating basilicas, each one anticipating the other with mutual honor, because where the command of love has enlarged hearts, the possession of peace does not become narrow. Then, when one of the two dies, from then on single bishops succeed single bishops according to the ancient custom. Nor will anything new happen; for from the very beginning of the separation, Catholic love has preserved this among those who, having condemned the error of wicked dissension, came to appreciate the sweetness of unity, even if late. Or if perhaps the Christian people delight in single bishops and cannot tolerate the partnership of two because of the unfamiliar appearance of things, let both of us withdraw from the middle, and let single bishops be appointed in the necessary places for single churches, once the cause of schism has been condemned and the churches established in peaceful unity, with single bishops in single churches consenting to unity."
notes: The source text contains a duplication: 'cuius examen cuius examen crirainationes' appears to be a scribal error with 'cuius examen' repeated and 'crirainationes' likely a corruption of 'criminationes' (accusations). The gloss renders the intended sense.

problems.why: glossary: banned rendering 'party of Donatus' (use 'Donatist party')
lint glossary: banned rendering of pars Donati; use 'Donatist party' ('party of Donatus')

edits.old: and remained only in the party of Donatus
edits.new: and remained only in the Donatist party

fixed: Replaced 'party of Donatus' with 'Donatist party' per glossary for pars Donati.

problems.quote: bearing fruit and growing in the whole world (Colossians 1:6)
problems.source_quote: sicut scriptum est toto mundo fructificantem atque crescentem
problems.why: Colossians 1:6 speaks of the gospel, not the Church; this allusion matches Acts 12:24 or similar growth passages, not Colossians.
problems.fix: bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, as it is written

edits.old: bearing fruit and growing in the whole world (Colossians 1:6)
edits.new: bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, as it is written

fixed: Removed the incorrect Colossians 1:6 citation; the source only says 'sicut scriptum est' (as it is written) without specifying a book, so the English should not supply one.

last_rejected.quote: we will owe them the grace of so great a benefit for the truth we have recognized
last_rejected.source_quote: quibus tanti gratiam beneficii pro cognita ueritate debebimus
last_rejected.why: Agency reversed: 'we will owe them' should be 'we will owe to them' (dative of person), but 'pro cognita veritate' means 'for the truth having been made known' (by them to us), not 'we have recognized'. The sense is 'for truth having been recognized/made known'.
last_rejected.fix: to whom we will owe the grace of so great a benefit for the truth made known
last_rejected.ruling: 'pro cognita veritate' = 'for recognized truth'; 'we have recognized' is within normal range. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the question of those very men whom they wanted to accuse rather than were able to convict has been settled
last_rejected.source_quote: quaestionem definitam, quamuis non in eis ecclesia consistat
last_rejected.why: Missing causal connection: 'quaestionem definitam' goes with what precedes (the settled question of Caecilian etc. proves the point), not a new condition. 'quamuis non in eis ecclesia consistat' = 'although the Church does not consist in them' is parenthetical, but the syntax shows this is all part of the protasis continuing from 'si denique'.
last_rejected.fix: if finally the question of those whom they then wished to accuse rather than could convict has been settled—though the Church does not consist in them
last_rejected.ruling: English keeps 'if...if...if' chain and parenthetical 'although Church does not consist in them'. No meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: by that emperor to whose examination they sent their accusations by their own choice
last_rejected.source_quote: ab eo imperatore, ad cuius examen cuius examen crirainationes suas ultro accusando miserunt
last_rejected.why: Source has dittography 'cuius examen cuius examen' but clearly 'ultro accusando' = 'by voluntarily accusing' (themselves initiating prosecution), not 'by their own choice' sending accusations. They voluntarily brought charges.
last_rejected.fix: by that emperor before whose examination they voluntarily brought their accusations
last_rejected.ruling: 'ultro accusando' = 'by voluntarily accusing'; 'by their own choice' conveys same sense adequately.

last_rejected.quote: let them hold unity with us in such a way that they not only find the way of salvation but do not lose the honor of a bishopric
last_rejected.source_quote: sic eius nobiscum teneant unitatem, ut non solum uiam salutis inueniant, sed nec honorem episcopatus amittant
last_rejected.why: 'eius...unitatem' = 'hold unity of it' (the Church), not 'unity with us'—though 'nobiscum' is there, 'eius' refers to the Church's unity. More seriously, 'ut non solum...sed nec' = 'so that they not only...but also not'—the 'nec' = 'and not', making this a promise of benefit, but 'amittant' = 'lose' is subjunctive of feared result/prevented result. The structure 'non solum...sed nec' is unusual; it means 'not only find salvation but [also] not lose honor'.
last_rejected.fix: let them so hold unity of it with us that they not only find the way of salvation but do not even lose the honor of a bishopric
last_rejected.ruling: 'unity with us' captures 'eius nobiscum unitatem'; 'not only...but also not lose' renders 'non solum...sed nec' correctly.

last_rejected.quote: Each one of us, joined with a colleague in honor, will be able to sit in turn in the more prominent seat, as when a foreign bishop sits beside a colleague
last_rejected.source_quote: poterit quippe unusquisque nostrum honoris sibi socio copulato uicissim sedere eminentius, sicut peregrino episcopo iuxta considente collega
last_rejected.why: Wrong subject: 'peregrino episcopo...considente collega' = 'with a visiting bishop sitting beside a colleague'—the colleague is the host, the peregrinus is visitor. 'sibi socio copulato' = 'joined with a partner for himself'. The simile compares the alternating honor to when a visiting bishop sits with a colleague (host).
last_rejected.fix: Each of us will be able to sit more prominently in turn, joined with a partner in honor, as when a visiting bishop sits beside a colleague
last_rejected.ruling: 'as when a foreign bishop sits beside a colleague' correctly renders 'sicut peregrino episcopo iuxta considente collega'. No major error.

last_rejected.quote: This is granted to both sides in alternating basilicas, each one anticipating the other with mutual honor
last_rejected.source_quote: hoc cum alternis basilicis utrimque conceditur utroque alterum cum honore mutuo praeueniente
last_rejected.why: 'utroque alterum...praeueniente' = 'with each anticipating the other'—but 'hoc...conceditur' = 'this is granted' is wrong voice; better 'this is arranged/agreed'. 'cum' = 'when' not 'in'. The ablative absolute describes the arrangement, not a grant.
last_rejected.fix: This is arranged when both sides alternate basilicas, each anticipating the other with mutual honor
last_rejected.ruling: 'conceditur' can mean 'granted'; 'cum' as 'when/in' is minor. Meaning preserved adequately.

last_rejected.quote: with single bishops in single churches consenting to unity
last_rejected.source_quote: ab episcopis singulis in ecclesiis singulis annuentibus unitati
last_rejected.why: Wrong syntax: 'ab episcopis...annuentibus' = 'with single bishops in single churches nodding/assenting to unity'—but this goes with 'constitutis', describing the state after both withdraw. However 'annuentibus unitati' = 'assenting to unity' is active (the bishops give assent), not 'consenting to unity' as a state. The real issue: 'utrique de medio discedamus' = 'let both of us withdraw from the middle'—'utrique' = both groups, not 'both of us' (Augustine and Marcellinus?).
last_rejected.fix: let both groups withdraw from the middle, and for single churches established in peaceful unity once the cause of schism has been condemned, let single bishops be appointed in the necessary places, with single bishops in single churches assenting to unity
last_rejected.ruling: 'consenting to unity' renders 'annuentibus unitati' adequately; 'both of us' for 'utrique' is acceptable in epistolary context.
